full_judgment:
AHM Shamsuddin Chowdhury J: This First Appeal is directed against the judgment and the decree dated 20-11-1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge of the First Commercial Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 66 of 1992. By the said judgment and the decree the learned Subordinate Judge refused to grant any relief the plaintiff asked for. 

 9. We felt inclined to address, at the very first instance, the question as to whether the reliefs sought by way of an order for reinstatement and by way of a mandatory injunction as well as by way of a declaration to the effect that the termination is invalid and ineffective can be granted. As is rightly accepted by the learned Advocates representing both the parties the relationship between the plaintiff and the defendants, was, at the relevant date, regulated purely by contractual terms though, some pre-existing statutory and subordinate legislative provisions had become parts of the contract by adoption, along with the instrument called Rupali Bank Employees Service Regulations 1981 which contain bulk of the contractual terms. This is because, as on that date the bank was no longer a statutory functionary or a government emanation. It is worthwhile, in this context. to stress that an award of pecuniary compensation by way of "damages" is the normal and the ordinary way of repairing loss suffered by an innocent party because of a breach of contract committed by the other. The reason being that the Common Law knew no other device of reparation. Chancery Court, however, at subsequent stages innovated other forms of relief, namely, specific performance, injunction, etc. But as we all know equitable remedies are not ordinary remedies, but are discretionary ones and are available only when Common Law remedies prove to be deficient and when conditions attached to the extra-ordinary remedies under equity are satisfied. From its very inception the Chancellor had insisted that equitable remedy of specific performance of contract shall be available only in a limited number of situations, and that the same would not be available in a number of circumstances, one of which is contract of personal service, the reason being that specific performance of such a contract would be tantamount to granting licence to slavery as far as an award to an employer is concerned and to clog an employer's freedom to get rid of an undesirable employee as far as an award to an employee is concerned. The doctrine of specific performance of contract is based on the maxim "Equity regards as done what ought to be done" and it was felt that a contract of personal service ought not to be regarded as done, When these principles, stemming from the Court of the Lord High Chancellor, travelled to our part of the world, albeit in codified form, almost all the precursory requirements remained unaffected. So, section 21 (b) of the Specific Relief Act, states in no ambiguous terms that a contract involving personal volition cannot be specifically enforced. The legal position in this respect has been lucidity and succinctly described in the case of Azizur Rahman vs Burman Oil Company, 13 DLR 458. As a corollary to the said principle, neither a declaration about a right of continuous service nor an order of injunction to pave way for the resumption of employment, which is bound to have the effect of indirect specific enforcement of a contract of personal service, can be granted. Hence, a decree, compelling the defendant No.1 directly or in a roundabout way, to reinstate the plaintiff, cannot be granted. In view of this finding there remains no necessity to make any pronouncement as to the validity of the amendment made to the plaint, because the reliefs barred by the Specific Relief Act are all that were sought by the amendment. We would, nevertheless, like to add that although there is a wealth of authority to back up the proposition that a pleading can be amended to insert new facts or new relief to correspond to subsequent revelation emerging from the written statement or from such evidence which was hitherto unknown before being divulged by the defendant (Sarat Chand Mitter vs Sreemuthy Mohun Bibi, 1898, 2 CWN 201, Riding vs Hawking 1889, 14 PD 56, Mihir Dutta vs Anadi Lal Kukherjee AIR 1980 Cal 339), the present one is not a case where that principle can be invoked, because the new reliefs are proscribed by sections 21 and 56 of the Specific Relief Act. We also deem it prudent to iterate that having incessantly perused the written statement, we arrived at the view, and for that purpose took as guide. the Appellate Division's decision in the case of Bangladesh Balik vs Mohammad Abdul Mannan, 46 DLR(AD) 1, that it would not be possible to infer from the contents in the written statement, without stretching the same far beyond the acceptable limit, that the plaintiff/appellant's termination was, in fact, a masqueraded dismissal. While it is true that some allegation of culpabable nature, surfacing from the written statement for the first time, have been labeled, but they have been resorted to for the only purpose of blocking some dues the plaintiff/appellant claims. Nothing indicates, or is capable of leading to the inference, that the plaintiff was terminated because of the said allegations. 

 28. The learned trial Judge's judgment and the decree, so far as the same relates to refusal to grant reliefs other than mandatory injunction, declaration, reinstatement as well as LPR benefit are concerned, is set aside, while his judgment in respect of mandatory injunction, declaration, reinstatement and LPR benefit is affirmed.
